Winchester.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of England's ancient capital
s1loc: Winchester runs a strong visitor economy as the former capital of England, anchored by Winchester Cathedral, a Norman foundation of 1070 with the longest medieval nave in Europe, the grave of Jane Austen and the 12th-century Winchester Bible. The Great Hall, the only surviving part of Winchester Castle, has housed King Arthur's legendary Round Table for over 700 years, while the City Mill and the Westgate draw heritage visitors year-round.

The leisure and activity layer follows the chalk streams through the city. Winnall Moors, a wetland nature reserve where the River Itchen flows through the centre, offers boardwalk and riverside walks, while the riverbanks down to St Cross, the water meadows and the South Downs Way and St Swithun's Way trails on the city's edge give walkers, cyclists and activity operators a busy outdoor offer through the warmer season.

Heritage and culture run deep here. The Theatre Royal Winchester on Jewry Street, a restored cine-variety theatre, and the City Hall stage a full programme, while the Hat Fair, the UK's longest-running outdoor arts festival, fills the streets each July. Winchester's Military Museums at Peninsula Barracks, including the Gurkha Museum and Horse Power, and the medieval streets around the High Street and the Buttercross add depth to the cultural draw.

Underpinning it all is a hotel, guest-house and inn trade serving heritage visitors, business travellers and walkers, with a guide and walking-tour scene built around the cathedral and the castle. Winchester station puts the city on the South Western main line, with London Waterloo around 55 minutes, Southampton 15 and Basingstoke 20, while the M3 carries day-trippers in for the cathedral city and the surrounding Hampshire downs.

Beeston.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of Greater Nottingham
s1loc: Beeston carries a green visitor economy on the south-western edge of Nottingham, anchored by the Attenborough Nature Reserve, 220 hectares of former gravel pits opened by Sir David Attenborough in 1966 and now a complex of lakes, wetlands and grassland with the award-winning Attenborough Nature Centre at its heart. The reserve draws thousands of birdwatchers, walkers and families year-round to the banks of the River Trent on the town's doorstep.

The leisure and activity layer runs along the water. Beeston Marina and the Beeston Canal towpath link to Beeston Lock and the Canalside Heritage Centre, which tells the story of the Nottingham and Beeston Canal, while the Big Track cycle route winds from Beeston Lock to Trent Bridge through the city. The University Park boating lake and the riverside trails keep walkers, anglers and cyclists busy across the warmer season.

Heritage and culture centre on the University of Nottingham's University Park campus, with the Djanogly Art Gallery and the Lakeside Arts centre staging music, theatre and exhibitions beside the lake. The town's historic Boots site at Beeston, with its Grade I listed modernist buildings by engineer Owen Williams, the redeveloped Beeston Square with its eight-screen Arc cinema, and the events around the canal fill the calendar through the year.

Underpinning it all is a hotel and guest-house trade serving the two universities, business parks and visitors heading into Nottingham, with a guide and day-trip scene built around the nature reserve and the Trent. The Nottingham Express Transit tram reached Beeston in 2015, linking the Beeston Interchange through the city to Hucknall, while Beeston station and the A52 carry day-trippers in from across the East Midlands.

Ayr.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of the Ayrshire coast
s1loc: Ayr runs a busy visitor economy on Scotland's south-west coast, anchored by Ayr Beach and its long Esplanade, with golden sands and views across the Firth of Clyde to the Isle of Arran. Just outside town at Alloway, the Robert Burns Birthplace Museum draws visitors to the thatched cottage where the poet was born, alongside the Auld Kirk, the Brig o' Doon and the Burns Monument, while the medieval Auld Brig and Wallace Tower mark the historic centre.

The leisure and activity layer reaches across the parks and shore. Belleisle Park and Rozelle Estate, the old Alloway estates south of the town, offer woodland, gardens and ponds, with the Maclaurin Art Gallery set within Rozelle. Ayr Racecourse, established in 1777, stages both flat and National Hunt fixtures, while the beach watersports, the seafront walks and the trails along the River Ayr keep families and activity operators busy through the season.

Heritage and culture centre on the Gaiety Theatre, built in 1902 and one of Scotland's iconic auditoriums, now run as a social enterprise staging ballet, opera, pantomime and live music. The Auld Kirk of Ayr where Burns was baptised, the High Street's Wallace Tower, and the events calendar built around the Burns connection give the town a strong cultural identity across the year and well beyond the summer months.

Underpinning it all is a hotel and guest-house trade serving coast visitors, golfers and Burns pilgrims, with a guide and tour scene built around Alloway and the Heritage Park. Ayr station and the A77 link the town to Glasgow, Kilmarnock and Irvine, while Glasgow Prestwick International Airport sits just two miles north, so operators handle stopover and inbound trade as well as day-trippers heading along the Ayrshire coast.

Kilmarnock.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of East Ayrshire
s1loc: Kilmarnock carries a strong visitor economy at the heart of East Ayrshire, anchored by Dean Castle Country Park, more than 200 acres in the centre of town around a recently renovated 14th-century castle housing world-class collections of arms, armour, tapestries and early musical instruments. The park's Rural Life Centre, urban farm with llamas and goats, adventure playground and the Treehouse Cafe at the visitor centre draw families year-round to free woodland walks.

The leisure and activity layer spreads across the parks and surrounding hills. Kay Park, with its boating loch and the imposing Burns Monument opened in 1879, offers open green space in the centre, while the woodland trails and the Dean Castle circular walks give walkers and activity operators a busy outdoor offer. The wider East Ayrshire countryside and the Loudoun estate near the town add to the seasonal draw for visitors.

Heritage and culture run deep here. The Dick Institute, opened in 1901, holds the largest museum and gallery spaces in Ayrshire and draws over 120,000 visitors a year, while Kilmarnock's standing as the birthplace of the Johnnie Walker whisky brand, established by John Walker in 1820, shapes the town's identity. The Burns connection, the poet's first published edition printed here, and the events calendar fill the diary through the year.

Underpinning it all is a hotel and guest-house trade serving visitors, business travellers and tourists touring Ayrshire, with a guide and day-trip scene built around Dean Castle and the Burns and Walker heritage. Kilmarnock station and the A71 and A77 link the town to Glasgow, Ayr and Irvine, so operators handle stopover trade as well as day-trippers heading for the country park and the wider East Ayrshire countryside.

Bridgwater.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of Sedgemoor
s1loc: Bridgwater runs a distinctive visitor economy in the heart of Sedgemoor, best known for the Bridgwater Guy Fawkes Carnival, one of the largest illuminated parades in Europe, which fills the November streets with elaborate floats and the unique squibbing display. The Bridgwater and Taunton Canal threads through the town with its willow-lined towpath, while the Somerset Brick and Tile Museum preserves the last surviving kiln of a once-major local industry on the Parrett.

The leisure and activity layer reaches into the surrounding hills and wetlands. The Quantock Hills, England's first designated Area of Outstanding Natural Beauty, offer walking, cycling and riding trails on the town's western edge, while the Somerset Levels around Burrowbridge and the WWT Steart Marshes nature reserve draw birdwatchers to spot cranes and herons. The canal towpath and country trails keep walkers and activity operators busy through the warmer season.

Heritage and culture centre on the Bridgwater Arts Centre, one of the oldest arts centres in the country, staging exhibitions, performances and workshops, and on the Carnival visitor centre at the Town Hall, which displays costumes, posters and squibs. The Bridgwater Fair each September, one of the largest fairs in the region, the historic Castle Street Georgian quarter and the events around the carnival fill the calendar through the year.

Underpinning it all is a hotel and inn trade serving visitors, business travellers and tourists heading for the coast and the hills, with a guide and tour scene built around the carnival and the Quantocks. Bridgwater station on the Bristol to Taunton line and junctions 23 and 24 of the M5 link the town to Taunton, Burnham-on-Sea and Weston-super-Mare, so operators handle day-trippers heading for the Somerset coast and the Levels.

Salisbury.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of south Wiltshire
s1loc: Salisbury runs a major visitor economy as a historic cathedral city, anchored by Salisbury Cathedral with its 123-metre spire, the tallest in the country, the world's oldest working clock and one of only four surviving 1215 originals of Magna Carta in its 13th-century Chapter House. The medieval Cathedral Close, the longest in Britain, and the Salisbury Museum with its renowned Stonehenge and archaeology collections draw heritage visitors from around the world year-round.

The leisure and activity layer reaches across the meadows and downs. The water-meadow footpaths to Harnham with their famous Constable view of the cathedral, the hillfort and Norman stronghold of Old Sarum two miles north, and the riverside walks where the Avon and Nadder meet give walkers, cyclists and activity operators a busy outdoor offer, with the surrounding Cranborne Chase landscape and country trails drawing visitors through the season.

Heritage and culture run deep here. The Salisbury Playhouse and the Salisbury Arts Centre, run by Wiltshire Creative, stage a full programme alongside the City Hall and the Salisbury International Arts Festival, while the twice-weekly Charter Market has filled the Market Place for over 800 years. Wilton House with its Palladian Bridge and Japanese water garden, and the festival calendar in the Close, give the city a rich cultural draw.

Underpinning it all is a deep hotel and guest-house trade serving heritage visitors and the Stonehenge tourist flow, with a guide and tour scene built around the cathedral and the prehistoric landscape. Salisbury station puts the city on the line to London Waterloo in around 90 minutes, while the Stonehenge Tour bus and the A303 and A36 carry day-trippers to the stone circle 12 kilometres north and across south Wiltshire.

Havant.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of the Hampshire coast
s1loc: Havant carries a busy visitor economy on the Hampshire coast between Portsmouth and Chichester, anchored by neighbouring Hayling Island, a traditional seaside resort with three miles of Blue Flag beaches along the Solent and the distinction as the birthplace of windsurfing. The island's Funland amusement park and the East Hayling Light Railway draw families through the season, while Langstone Harbour and its Hayling Ferry crossing add a busy waterside draw on the town's southern edge.

The leisure and activity layer centres on the award-winning Staunton Country Park, with its Victorian glasshouse of exotic plants, its maze and the ornamental farm where families feed the animals. The four-mile Hayling Billy coastal path along a former railway, the windsurfing, sailing and kitesurfing off Hayling, and the walking and cycling trails around the harbours give activity operators and families a strong outdoor offer across the warmer season.

Heritage and culture centre on the Spring Arts and Heritage Centre in the town centre, which stages theatre, film, music and exhibitions and houses the Havant Museum tracing local history from Roman times, including the town's parchment-making and textile past. The historic streets around St Faith's Church, the conservation areas at Langstone with its old mill and quay, and the events calendar fill the diary through the year.

Underpinning it all is a hotel and guest-house trade serving coast visitors, harbour sailors and travellers between Portsmouth and Chichester, with a guide and day-trip scene built around Hayling Island and the harbours. Havant station on the Portsmouth to London Waterloo line, the connection to the Chichester and West Sussex coast, and the A27 and A3(M) carry day-trippers in for the beaches, the country park and the Solent shore.
